A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Constrained Posterior Sampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between versions.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on stocks, traffic, air quality, and synthetic waveforms, including conditional settings, quantitative comparisons, and increasing-constraint analyses in Section 4.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, non-convex constraint experiments, imputation results, ablations, and inference-time measurements in Section 5 and the appendices.

M1.justification: The standard CPS algorithm, denoiser, projection objective, and exponential penalty schedule are retained. V2 adds an experimental noise-correction variant that recomputes the noise estimate from the projected posterior mean before the DDIM update (Section 3 and Appendix B.7). This is a limited procedural variant tested as an ablation, rather than a replacement for CPS.

E1.justification: The original datasets and six evaluation settings remain. V2 substantially extends task requirements through non-convex autocorrelation constraints combined with OHLC constraints on stocks and direct time-series imputation using observed-value constraints. The latter differs from v1's downstream imputation evaluation of synthetic training data.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with Diffusion-TS, PDM, PRODIGY, and Loss-DiffTime (Tables 1–3); v1 explicitly excluded Loss-DiffTime. Figure 5 also changes comparator membership: PDM and PRODIGY replace Guided DiffTime alongside the retained COP-FT comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds Discriminative Score and removes SSIM and constraint-violation-rate reporting. The new direct-imputation protocol uses 50% masking and MAE, while the existing TSTR protocol retains 75% masking. Guided DiffTime's stated weight-selection criterion changes from violation rate to violation magnitude; this documents a protocol revision without establishing that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained increasing-constraint analysis, v2 adds penalty-schedule comparisons, individual-constraint analyses, guidance-weight sensitivity results, and the noise-correction ablation (Appendix B). It also adds latency scaling and multiple generated samples for identical constraints (Appendices D and E), substantially expanding evidence about design choices, efficiency, and diversity.

E5.justification: Three-seed TSTR reporting is retained. V2 adds five-seed Discriminative Score results, timing summaries averaged over ten runs, and generated-sample mean and standard-deviation bands. Its checklist also explicitly identifies DTW dispersion as variation across test samples. These additions do not establish an increase in runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results in Tables 2–9 and Figures 7–11, adds DS entries, and removes SSIM and violation-rate entries. Retained CPS results in Table 1 are unchanged, but some comparator values change: COP's Air Quality FD changes from 0.2165 to 0.2206 and TSTR from 0.22 to 0.25. Table 8's Traffic CPS DTW conflicts with Table 1 and cannot establish a performance improvement.

T1.justification: The Gaussian/linear-constraint framework and most proofs are retained. V2 extends the existing convergence argument with an explicit O(1/T) rate statement and a tolerance-dependent choice of k (Theorem 4.4 and Appendix C.2), and adds projection-convergence discussion in Appendix D. It also replaces v1's formal maximum-likelihood objective with a typical constrained-sample formulation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains scalable, training-free constrained generation through posterior-mean projection. The abstract's headline changes from approximately 10% TSTR and 42% DTW improvements to 70% DS and 22% DTW improvements with expanded comparisons. The introduction also narrows its description of convergence analysis from convex constraints to linear constraints with Gaussian data.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of how projecting noisy latents can harm denoising and diversity, why noise correction may hurt CPS, and why performance can remain useful with non-convex constraints. It replaces the evaluation's emphasis on a unique matching test sample with distributional and per-sample comparisons, and explicitly discusses the Gaussian and unique-solution restrictions of its convergence results.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information: GPU hardware, training-epoch limits, checkpoint selection, conditional metadata fields, four-process projection parallelism, the DS classifier, and new baseline settings are documented. These are principally additional disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing training. V1 promises future code release; v2's checklist states that supplementary code and data are supplied, although their availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning around training-based versus training-free constrained generation, adding discussion of PDM, PRODIGY, Mirror Diffusion Models, and constrained-domain diffusion. It develops the distinction between projecting clean estimates and noisy latents and expands time-series diffusion coverage in Appendix A. The earlier GLACIER/COMET counterfactual discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The introduction, background, method explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work gains separate training-based and training-free subsections, theory becomes a standalone section, and results move from question-led discussion to organized findings. Appendices are reorganized, with new checklist, acknowledgements, and societal-impact material.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned, Figure 2 changes its headline metric, and Figure 5 is redrawn with different comparator curves. The qualitative grid is transposed and compressed, while v1 Figure 3 moves to the appendix as v2 Figure 6. Eight additional tables and five additional figures substantially expand the visual presentation, alongside the conference-format layout.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for CPS's central projection choice through comparisons with closely related projection methods, targeted ablations, non-convex constraints, and direct imputation tests. Runtime measurements and expanded implementation details address important gaps in v1's assessment of practicality and reproducibility. The Traffic DTW inconsistency between Tables 8 and 1 limits confidence in that ablation entry, but the broader gains in empirical support and transparency clearly outweigh this localized reporting problem.
